blocks.text: It is proved that צפע tsepha, or צפעני tsiphoni, is the regulus, or basilisk.

Of the serpent צפע tsepha, or צפעני tsiphoni, we read in Prov. XXIII, 32. At the last it will bite like a serpent, and sting like tsiphoni. And Esa. XI, 8. The sucking child shall play over the hole of the asp, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the den of tsiphoni. And Es. XIV, 29. Out of the serpent's root shall come forth tsepha. And Esa. LIX, 5. They hatch the eggs of tsiphoni, etc. He who eats of their eggs shall die; and if one crushes them, a viper will break out. And Ierem. VIII, 17. I will send among them serpents, tsiphonim, against which there is no charm; and they shall bite you, says the Lord. From these passages it is clear enough that these are very savage serpents. But to determine the species is not easy. The Greeks in some places render κεράστας [kerastas], in others ἀσπίδας [aspidas] and ἔγγονα ἀσπίδων [engona aspidōn], in others ὄφεις θανατοῦντας [opheis thanatountas]; the Chaldee consistently חורמנין hurmanim, as the Syriac mostly has ܚܘܪܡܢܝܢ hormanin, but once ܐܣܦܣ, asp, and once ܓܪܣܐ, amphisbaena. Aquila has βασιλίσκους [basiliskous], Jerome regulos, Münster hydros, Junius haemorrhoos, Castalio viperas. Kimchi says only that the serpent is הקשה והרע, harsh and evil, and Aquinas קשה ורע, harsh and dire.

We prefer Jerome's version to all of these. 1. Because among the ancients it has more supporters. For Aquila, by far the most accurate of all the translators, had led the way. To this is added the authority of the Chaldee paraphrast, who consistently renders חורמן hurman, as the Syriac mostly has ܚܘܪܡܢ horman, that is, the regulus; like the Arabic حرمانا [ḥrmānā] harmene, by which word, it is agreed, either the regulus or a serpent very similar to the regulus is meant. For Avicenna relates that the bite of both is incurable, and that both harm not only by their bite but also by their gaze and hiss. Thus, as he had said of the basilisk, تقتل بصفيرها الي علوة ومن وقع عليه بصرها من بعيد مات [taqtul bi-ṣafīrihā ilā ghalwa wa-man waqaʿa ʿalayhi baṣaruhā min baʿīd māt] It kills with its hiss [col. 400] as far as a bowshot (the translator ineptly has if it raises itself). And he on whom its gaze falls from afar dies; so he writes of the harmene in the following chapter: قد ذكر حرمانا في صفات قريبة من صفات الملكة من انها لا تسوي وليس انما تقتل باللسع فقط بل باللحظ وباسماع الصفير [qad dhukira ḥrmānā fī ṣifāt qarība min ṣifāt al-malika min annahā lā tusawwī wa-laysa innamā taqtul bi-l-lasʿ faqaṭ bal bi-l-laḥẓ wa-bi-ismāʿ al-ṣafīr] It is indeed recorded that the harmene has attributes very close to the attributes of the basilisk, since it injures, or indeed kills, not by its bite alone, [III, 183] but also by its gaze and by the hearing of its hiss. Hence the Pandectarius: Harmene, basilisk. Likewise: Karmene (wrongly for Harmene) is a serpent that kills not only by its bite but by its gaze and by being heard, that is, by its hiss. Avicenna holds that they differ only in size, since the length of the basilisk is said to be شبران الي ثلثة [shibrān ilā thalātha] from two spans to three, but that of the harmene من ذراع الي ذراع ونصف [min dhirāʿ ilā dhirāʿ wa-niṣf] from one cubit to a cubit and a half. But here he has overlooked the relation of the measures. For شبر [shibr] is the greater span, in Greek σπιθαμὴ [spithamē], a measure of twelve fingers, which doubled makes a cubit. So a length of two to three spans is exactly the same as one of one to one and a half cubits. These two measures differ in words but agree in substance. Other Arabs, however, more correctly assign the basilisk only one شبر [shibr], that is, one σπιθαμὴν [spithamēn] of length. Alkazuinius in the chapter حية [ḥayya], or On Serpents: ومنها الحية تقال لها الملكة طولها شبرا واكثر [wa-minhā al-ḥayya tuqāl lahā al-malika ṭūluhā shibran wa-akthar] Among them also is the serpent Almelecha (or basilisk), whose length is a span (the greater) and more. So also Damir in the chapter الملكة [al-malika] Almelecha. Most of the ancients report what agrees with this. Nicander, Theriaca, verse 398.
Ξανθὸς, ἐπὶ τρία δῶρα φέρων μῆκός τε, καὶ ἰθὺν. [Xanthos, epi tria dōra pherōn mēkos te, kai ithyn.]
